units.title: CPU vs GPU Architecture
units.tip: CPUs and GPUs are both processors but designed for different jobs. A CPU has few powerful cores optimized for sequential execution and complex logic. A GPU has many simple cores designed for parallel work on identical tasks. This architectural difference makes GPUs ideal for tasks where the same operation runs on many data elements.

exercises.question: What is the primary design focus of a CPU?
exercises.answer: Sequential execution with complex logic and branch prediction
exercises.explain: CPUs are optimized to run one instruction stream very quickly with advanced features. They handle variable workloads, loops, and conditions efficiently.
choices: Processing many identical operations in parallel
Sequential execution with complex logic and branch prediction

exercises.question: What is the primary design focus of a GPU?
exercises.answer: Executing the same operation on many pieces of data in parallel
exercises.explain: GPUs have thousands of simple cores all doing the same work simultaneously. This is perfect for data-parallel tasks.
choices: Executing the same operation on many pieces of data in parallel

exercises.question: How many cores does a typical CPU have compared to a GPU?
exercises.answer: A CPU has few cores; a GPU has thousands
exercises.explain: CPUs typically have a handful to a few dozen cores. GPUs have thousands of simpler cores doing parallel work.
choices: It depends only on the year manufactured
A CPU has few cores; a GPU has thousands

exercises.question: What is 'latency hiding' in GPU design?
exercises.answer: Using many threads to keep cores busy while one thread waits for memory
exercises.explain: When memory access is slow, a GPU switches to another thread. With thousands of threads, there is always work available.
choices: Storing data very close to the CPU
Using many threads to keep cores busy while one thread waits for memory

exercises.question: Why do GPU cores run slower clock speeds than CPU cores?
exercises.answer: They are simpler designs optimized for volume and parallelism, not individual speed
exercises.explain: GPU cores are stripped-down, simple cores. Each core runs slower, but there are so many that throughput is much higher overall.
choices: They are simpler designs optimized for volume and parallelism, not individual speed
Modern GPUs run as fast as CPUs

exercises.question: What is an integrated GPU?
exercises.answer: A GPU built into the CPU or chipset, sharing system memory
exercises.explain: Integrated GPUs share RAM with the CPU, reducing cost and power but with lower bandwidth. They are common in laptops and mobile devices.
choices: A GPU built into the CPU or chipset, sharing system memory
A GPU that can only run one application
A GPU that only displays text

exercises.question: What is a dedicated GPU?
exercises.answer: A separate graphics card with its own dedicated memory
exercises.explain: Dedicated GPUs have their own VRAM, usually their own power input, and connect through a slot such as PCIe. They offer much higher performance than integrated GPUs.
choices: A GPU shared between multiple computers
A separate graphics card with its own dedicated memory
A GPU that can only run one application
A GPU that requires internet connection

exercises.question: What is the advantage of a dedicated GPU over an integrated one?
exercises.answer: Dedicated GPUs have more VRAM, higher bandwidth, and more processing power
exercises.explain: Dedicated cards have independent memory and computation resources, enabling much higher performance for demanding tasks.
choices: Dedicated GPUs have more VRAM, higher bandwidth, and more processing power

exercises.question: What is a PCIe slot?
exercises.answer: The connection standard that allows a dedicated GPU to connect to a motherboard
exercises.explain: PCIe (PCI Express) is the high-speed bus connecting expansion cards like dedicated GPUs to the motherboard.
choices: The connection standard that allows a dedicated GPU to connect to a motherboard

exercises.question: Why might someone choose an integrated GPU over a dedicated one?
exercises.answer: Lower cost, lower power consumption, and simpler installation for basic tasks
exercises.explain: Integrated GPUs are sufficient for everyday computing, web browsing, and light graphics work while using less power.
choices: Lower cost, lower power consumption, and simpler installation for basic tasks
Integrated GPUs have more dedicated memory

units.title: GPU Cores and Parallelism
units.tip: GPU cores are organized in groups that execute the same instruction on different data. Modern GPUs have thousands of these cores arranged in streaming multiprocessors. Each core is built around a simple arithmetic logic unit (ALU), and the multiprocessor provides registers, shared memory, and cache. The massive number of cores enables GPUs to perform trillions of operations per second.

exercises.question: What is a GPU core?
exercises.answer: A simple processor unit that performs basic arithmetic and logic operations
exercises.explain: GPU cores are simpler than CPU cores. Each has an ALU for computation, but lacks complex branch prediction and caching found in CPU cores.
choices: A simple processor unit that performs basic arithmetic and logic operations

exercises.question: What is SIMD execution?
exercises.answer: Single Instruction, Multiple Data: one instruction executes on many data elements simultaneously
exercises.explain: SIMD is the core idea behind GPU execution. A group of cores performs the same operation on different data in lockstep. Some vendors call their variant SIMT.
choices: Single Instruction, Multiple Data: one instruction executes on many data elements simultaneously

exercises.question: What is a warp or wavefront?
exercises.answer: A group of cores executing the same instruction in lockstep on different data
exercises.explain: A warp (in some GPU designs) or wavefront (in others) is a batch of threads all executing the same instruction simultaneously.
choices: A group of cores executing the same instruction in lockstep on different data

exercises.question: What is the purpose of GPU registers?
exercises.answer: Fast storage for a single core to hold intermediate computation results
exercises.explain: Registers are the fastest memory available, local to each core. They store values being actively computed.
choices: Fast storage for a single core to hold intermediate computation results

exercises.question: How many threads can a GPU typically keep in flight at once?
exercises.answer: Far more than its core count, often tens of thousands or more
exercises.explain: GPUs keep many more threads resident than they have cores, so that some are always ready to run while others wait on memory.
choices: The same as CPU core count
Far more than its core count, often tens of thousands or more

exercises.question: What is data parallelism?
exercises.answer: Running the same operation on many pieces of data simultaneously
exercises.explain: Data parallelism is the GPU's strength. Process millions of pixels, particles, or data elements with the same kernel in parallel.
choices: Storing data in parallel across networks
Running the same operation on many pieces of data simultaneously

exercises.question: What is a GPU thread?
exercises.answer: An independent execution context running a portion of a kernel program
exercises.explain: Each GPU thread runs the same kernel code, but on different data. A single kernel launch can create millions of threads.
choices: An independent execution context running a portion of a kernel program

exercises.question: What is a GPU kernel?
exercises.answer: A small program that runs on thousands of GPU threads in parallel
exercises.explain: A kernel is the function executed by every GPU thread. It processes one data element per thread.
choices: A small program that runs on thousands of GPU threads in parallel

exercises.question: What is 'occupancy' in GPU computing?
exercises.answer: The ratio of active warps to the maximum a GPU multiprocessor can hold
exercises.explain: High occupancy means a multiprocessor has many warps ready to run, which helps hide memory delays. Low occupancy leaves less work available to switch to.
choices: The ratio of active warps to the maximum a GPU multiprocessor can hold

exercises.question: Why do GPUs launch millions of threads despite having fewer cores?
exercises.answer: Threads block on memory; GPU switches to other threads, hiding latency
exercises.explain: When one thread waits for memory, the GPU schedules thousands of others. This keeps cores busy and hides memory delays.
choices: Threads block on memory; GPU switches to other threads, hiding latency

units.title: Graphics Pipeline on Hardware
units.tip: The graphics pipeline is a series of stages that transform 3D models into 2D images on screen. Geometry is processed, then rasterized into pixels, then colored through shading. Some stages use fixed-function hardware, such as rasterization, while the programmable stages run as shaders on the GPU cores.

exercises.question: What is the graphics pipeline?
exercises.answer: A series of hardware stages that convert 3D models into pixels on screen
exercises.explain: The pipeline includes vertex processing, rasterization, fragment shading, and output merging. Each stage is optimized for its job.
choices: A series of hardware stages that convert 3D models into pixels on screen

exercises.question: What is vertex processing?
exercises.answer: The stage that transforms 3D vertex positions and prepares per-vertex data
exercises.explain: Vertex processing takes 3D coordinates and transforms them based on the camera and object position. It can also compute data such as normals and texture coordinates.
choices: The stage that transforms 3D vertex positions and prepares per-vertex data

exercises.question: What is rasterization?
exercises.answer: Converting 3D geometric shapes into 2D pixels for the screen
exercises.explain: Rasterization determines which screen pixels are covered by each triangle or polygon, preparing them for color computation.
choices: Converting 3D geometric shapes into 2D pixels for the screen

exercises.question: What is a fragment in the graphics pipeline?
exercises.answer: A candidate pixel produced by rasterization that may or may not appear in the final image
exercises.explain: Fragments are potential pixels. Shading and depth testing determine which fragments actually contribute to the final image.
choices: A candidate pixel produced by rasterization that may or may not appear in the final image

exercises.question: What is the final stage of the graphics pipeline?
exercises.answer: Output merging, which combines fragments into the final pixel colors in the framebuffer
exercises.explain: Output merging performs depth testing, blending, and writes final colors to video memory for display.
choices: Output merging, which combines fragments into the final pixel colors in the framebuffer

exercises.question: What is a shader?
exercises.answer: A program that runs on GPU hardware to compute colors, positions, or other visual attributes
exercises.explain: Shaders are small programs. Vertex shaders process vertices; fragment shaders compute pixel colors. They run in parallel on thousands of cores.
choices: A program that runs on GPU hardware to compute colors, positions, or other visual attributes

exercises.question: What is a vertex shader?
exercises.answer: A program that runs once per vertex, transforming positions and calculating per-vertex properties
exercises.explain: Vertex shaders execute in parallel on every vertex. They transform coordinates, compute lighting contributions, and prepare data for rasterization.
choices: A program that processes every pixel
A program that runs once per vertex, transforming positions and calculating per-vertex properties

exercises.question: What is a fragment shader?
exercises.answer: A program that runs once per fragment, computing the final color for that screen pixel
exercises.explain: Fragment shaders run in parallel on millions of fragments. They determine colors based on textures, lighting, and other inputs.
choices: A program that runs once per fragment, computing the final color for that screen pixel
A program that reads keyboard input

exercises.question: What is 'shader compilation'?
exercises.answer: Converting shader source code into machine instructions for the GPU
exercises.explain: Shaders are compiled by the GPU driver into code the GPU can execute. This happens at runtime or offline.
choices: Converting shader source code into machine instructions for the GPU

exercises.question: What does 'branching' in shaders mean?
exercises.answer: Using if-then-else logic where different threads may take different code paths
exercises.explain: Branching can be slow on GPUs when threads in the same warp take different paths, because the hardware must run each path in turn. This is called divergence and reduces parallelism.
choices: Using if-then-else logic where different threads may take different code paths

units.title: GPU Memory Hierarchy
units.tip: GPUs have multiple levels of memory with different speeds and sizes. Register memory is fastest but smallest, local to each core. Shared memory is fast and shared within a work group. Global memory is large but slower. The memory hierarchy is crucial to GPU performance: accessing register or shared memory is fast; accessing global memory takes hundreds of cycles.

exercises.question: What is VRAM in a GPU?
exercises.answer: Video RAM, the main memory attached to the GPU for storing textures, models, and framebuffers
exercises.explain: VRAM is dedicated memory on the graphics card. It holds all data the GPU needs: images, geometry, and computed results.
choices: Video RAM, the main memory attached to the GPU for storing textures, models, and framebuffers
Virtual RAM on the hard drive

exercises.question: What is GPU memory bandwidth?
exercises.answer: The amount of data that can be read from or written to memory per unit time
exercises.explain: Bandwidth is critical to GPU performance. GPUs prioritize bandwidth over latency, with wide memory buses accessing gigabytes per second.
choices: The amount of data that can be read from or written to memory per unit time

exercises.question: What are GPU registers?
exercises.answer: The fastest memory, local to each core, storing active computation values
exercises.explain: Registers are on-core memory with the lowest access time. Space is limited, so each thread can use only a limited number of registers.
choices: The fastest memory, local to each core, storing active computation values

exercises.question: What is shared memory on a GPU?
exercises.answer: Fast memory shared by all cores in a thread block or work group
exercises.explain: Shared memory is faster than global memory but slower than registers. Multiple cores can access it, enabling data sharing within a group.
choices: System RAM accessed by the GPU
Fast memory shared by all cores in a thread block or work group

exercises.question: What is cache memory on a GPU?
exercises.answer: Transparent hardware that automatically stores recently accessed memory to speed access
exercises.explain: GPU caches (L1, L2) automatically keep frequently accessed data nearby, reducing average memory latency.
choices: Memory you manage manually in code
Transparent hardware that automatically stores recently accessed memory to speed access

exercises.question: What is 'coalesced memory access'?
exercises.answer: When multiple threads access adjacent memory locations, allowing efficient parallel reads
exercises.explain: Coalescing combines multiple memory requests into fewer transactions. It is crucial for GPU performance.
choices: When multiple threads access adjacent memory locations, allowing efficient parallel reads

exercises.question: What happens with non-coalesced memory access?
exercises.answer: Multiple memory transactions are needed for what could be a single transaction, reducing efficiency
exercises.explain: When threads access scattered locations, the GPU must issue many separate memory requests, wasting bandwidth.
choices: Multiple memory transactions are needed for what could be a single transaction, reducing efficiency

exercises.question: What is memory striding?
exercises.answer: Accessing memory at regular intervals, which can prevent coalescing if the stride is poor
exercises.explain: If threads access every nth element, they may not coalesce. Choosing stride carefully is important for performance.
choices: Accessing memory at regular intervals, which can prevent coalescing if the stride is poor

exercises.question: What is 'bank conflict' in shared memory?
exercises.answer: When multiple threads access different addresses in the same memory bank at once, serializing the access
exercises.explain: Shared memory is divided into banks. If several threads hit different addresses in the same bank, the requests serialize, reducing parallelism.
choices: When multiple threads access different addresses in the same memory bank at once, serializing the access

exercises.question: Why is memory access pattern optimization important for GPU performance?
exercises.answer: Memory throughput is a bottleneck; efficient patterns maximize parallelism and bandwidth utilization
exercises.explain: CPUs rely on deep caches to hide memory delays. GPUs rely on bandwidth and many threads, making access patterns critical to performance.
choices: Memory throughput is a bottleneck; efficient patterns maximize parallelism and bandwidth utilization
It allows code to be human-readable

units.title: General-Purpose GPU Computing
units.tip: GPUs are not just for graphics. General-Purpose GPU (GPGPU) computing uses GPUs for scientific simulations, machine learning, data processing, and other compute tasks. The same massive parallelism that renders images can train neural networks or simulate physics. GPGPU frameworks allow programmers to write general compute kernels that run on GPU cores.

exercises.question: What is GPGPU computing?
exercises.answer: Using GPUs for general-purpose compute tasks beyond graphics rendering
exercises.explain: GPGPU leverages the same parallel hardware for machine learning, scientific computing, signal processing, and data analysis.
choices: Using GPUs for general-purpose compute tasks beyond graphics rendering

exercises.question: How do GPUs accelerate machine learning?
exercises.answer: Neural network computations involve massive matrix operations that GPUs execute in parallel
exercises.explain: Training and inference require multiplying huge matrices. GPUs execute millions of independent multiplications simultaneously.
choices: Machine learning runs only on CPUs
Neural network computations involve massive matrix operations that GPUs execute in parallel
GPUs store the training data more cheaply

exercises.question: What is a compute shader?
exercises.answer: A shader program that performs general computations, not tied to graphics
exercises.explain: Compute shaders run arbitrary parallel algorithms. They are decoupled from the graphics pipeline.
choices: A shader program that performs general computations, not tied to graphics
A shader that requires a monitor
A shader that only works on textures

exercises.question: What types of problems benefit most from GPU acceleration?
exercises.answer: Data-parallel problems with millions of independent operations on structured data
exercises.explain: GPUs excel when the same operation runs on many data elements. Simulations, machine learning, and image processing are ideal.
choices: Data-parallel problems with millions of independent operations on structured data

exercises.question: Why might a problem not benefit from GPU acceleration?
exercises.answer: If it requires sequential processing, has many branches, or data transfers overshadow computation
exercises.explain: GPUs are worst at sequential workloads, heavily branched code, and moving data on and off the card.
choices: If it requires sequential processing, has many branches, or data transfers overshadow computation

exercises.question: What is a GPU computing framework?
exercises.answer: A programming interface allowing you to write parallel compute kernels for GPUs
exercises.explain: Frameworks abstract the GPU hardware, letting programmers write compute programs without low-level graphics knowledge.
choices: A programming interface allowing you to write parallel compute kernels for GPUs
A physical building for GPU servers

exercises.question: What do compute shaders and compute frameworks such as OpenCL have in common?
exercises.answer: Both let programmers run general computation on the GPU
exercises.explain: Compute shaders live inside graphics APIs, while frameworks such as OpenCL are separate compute-focused interfaces. Both run parallel kernels on GPU hardware.
choices: Both let programmers run general computation on the GPU

exercises.question: Why is data transfer between CPU and GPU important to performance?
exercises.answer: Transferring data to the GPU takes time; if computation time is short, transfer overhead dominates
exercises.explain: PCIe bandwidth is much lower than GPU memory bandwidth. Large transfers can negate acceleration benefits.
choices: Transferring data to the GPU takes time; if computation time is short, transfer overhead dominates

exercises.question: What is 'arithmetic intensity' in GPU computing?
exercises.answer: The ratio of arithmetic operations to memory access, indicating GPU utilization potential
exercises.explain: High arithmetic intensity means lots of computation per byte loaded. Low intensity means memory bottleneck dominates.
choices: The ratio of arithmetic operations to memory access, indicating GPU utilization potential

exercises.question: When is GPU acceleration most valuable for a compute task?
exercises.answer: When arithmetic intensity is high and the algorithm is data-parallel
exercises.explain: High arithmetic intensity means computation outweighs memory transfer overhead. Data parallelism matches GPU strengths.
choices: When arithmetic intensity is high and the algorithm is data-parallel

units.title: Power and Cooling
units.tip: GPUs consume significant electrical power, generating substantial heat. Power consumption scales with the number of cores and clock speed. Heat dissipation requires effective cooling: massive heatsinks and fans, or liquid cooling in extreme cases. Power delivery must be robust to avoid voltage drops that reduce performance or stability.

exercises.question: What determines GPU power consumption?
exercises.answer: Number of cores active, clock speed, and voltage supplied to the chip
exercises.explain: Power use scales with core count and clock frequency. Voltage has a quadratic effect, so even small reductions save significant power.
choices: Number of cores active, clock speed, and voltage supplied to the chip

exercises.question: What is 'throttling' in GPU operation?
exercises.answer: Automatically reducing clock speed or voltage to stay within power and thermal limits
exercises.explain: Throttling prevents overheating and power supply failure. It trades performance for stability when thermal limits approach.
choices: Automatically reducing clock speed or voltage to stay within power and thermal limits

exercises.question: Why do many high-end dedicated GPUs require external power connectors?
exercises.answer: The PCIe slot supplies only limited power, so additional connectors deliver the rest
exercises.explain: High-end GPUs can draw hundreds of watts, but the PCIe slot supplies only a small share of that. Extra connectors deliver the rest.
choices: The PCIe slot supplies only limited power, so additional connectors deliver the rest

exercises.question: What is 'power efficiency' in GPUs?
exercises.answer: How much computation is performed per unit of electrical power consumed
exercises.explain: Efficiency measures performance per watt. Better efficiency means less heat and lower electricity bills.
choices: How much computation is performed per unit of electrical power consumed

exercises.question: What is 'dynamic voltage and frequency scaling' (DVFS)?
exercises.answer: Adjusting voltage and clock speed in real time based on workload to save power
exercises.explain: DVFS lowers power consumption during light loads and boosts it for demanding work, balancing performance and efficiency.
choices: Adjusting voltage and clock speed in real time based on workload to save power

exercises.question: Why do GPUs require cooling systems?
exercises.answer: High power consumption generates heat; cooling prevents overheating and ensures reliable operation
exercises.explain: Modern GPUs are compact but consume hundreds of watts. Without cooling, silicon temperature would exceed operational limits.
choices: High power consumption generates heat; cooling prevents overheating and ensures reliable operation
Because data centers prefer cold rooms

exercises.question: What is a heatsink in GPU cooling?
exercises.answer: A metal structure with large surface area that transfers heat from the GPU to the air
exercises.explain: Heatsinks use fins to increase surface area. Air passing through carries heat away from the GPU.
choices: A metal structure with large surface area that transfers heat from the GPU to the air

exercises.question: What is thermal paste in GPU installation?
exercises.answer: A conductive material placed between the GPU and heatsink to improve heat transfer
exercises.explain: Thermal paste fills microscopic gaps, creating better contact and allowing heat to flow efficiently to the heatsink.
choices: A conductive material placed between the GPU and heatsink to improve heat transfer

exercises.question: What is liquid cooling in GPUs?
exercises.answer: Circulating liquid through channels to absorb and transport GPU heat away efficiently
exercises.explain: Liquid cooling handles extreme heat loads better than air cooling. It is common in overclocked systems and data centres.
choices: Circulating liquid through channels to absorb and transport GPU heat away efficiently
Using water to power the GPU

exercises.question: What is the junction temperature of a GPU?
exercises.answer: The maximum safe operating temperature at the silicon junction where transistors operate
exercises.explain: Exceeding junction temperature can damage the chip, so GPUs throttle first. Limits are roughly 85 to 110 degrees Celsius depending on the model.
choices: The room temperature where the GPU sits
The maximum safe operating temperature at the silicon junction where transistors operate
